curated.x: KRIOS makes short documentaries on Greek history, faith and family memory, for Greeks in Greece and everywhere else. It describes itself as the living story of Greek civilization, with five aims: preserve, teach, understand, connect, pass forward.

curated.q: How does KRIOS decide what goes into a film?
curated.x: KRIOS says that if a claim cannot be traced to a source, it does not go in the film, and when the evidence runs out, the film says so. It prefers the oldest source to the most famous one, using primary sources and named scholarship for historical claims, checked before recording and again on the finished film.

curated.q: How does KRIOS keep history, tradition and belief apart?
curated.x: KRIOS says it separates what is documented, what the Church teaches, what families practice, and where communities differ. In this Guide, answers about contested or inherited subjects carry the labels HISTORY, TRADITION, BELIEF or PRACTICE so you can see which kind of statement you are reading.

KRIOS says it uses real archives first, credited with their licence. Where no photograph exists, some everyday scenes are illustrated. Those are marked, as with the labelled illustration on the home page, and they never stand in for sacred or historical evidence.

curated.q: Who narrates the films, and are there captions?
curated.x: KRIOS says every documentary today is narrated in a human voice, and that new films get English and Greek captions reviewed by people.

The newest film is The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried (9 minutes, released October 18, 2026, Living Roots), about families who left Greece and what they carried with them. The film before it, The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was (11 minutes, October 11, 2026), is about dance, memory and what makes a tradition survive.

Sacred Days are KRIOS films released on the day of a feast or name day, on faith, customs and the traditions families carry forward. The Sacred Days page lists a curated calendar of feast days and says the Saint Demetrios film premieres on YouTube on Monday, October 26, 2026, the feast day.

curated.q: Why did Greeks leave Greece between 1890 and 1914?
curated.x: The Migration Policy Institute says the first wave of emigration was spurred by the economic crisis of 1893, after a rapid fall in the price of currants. From 1890 to 1914 almost a sixth of the population of Greece emigrated, mostly to the United States and Egypt.

curated.q: What was the second wave of Greek emigration?
curated.x: According to the Migration Policy Institute, more than one million Greeks emigrated in a second wave, mainly between 1950 and 1974, to Western Europe, the United States, Canada and Australia. It also says almost half of the post-war emigrants had returned to Greece.

curated.q: How many Greeks reached the United States in the first wave?
curated.x: This is still an open question on the film page. It notes that published histories give figures from about 430,000 to more than 600,000, so the film says only "hundreds of thousands". No single approved source settles the number, so the Guide does not give one.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.h: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: October 18, 2026 · 9 min A suitcase can carry clothes and photographs. How do you pack a language, a song, or a church bell? Illustration from the film. Have you ever heard someone in your family mention a village in Greece, or an island, and realized you never asked what life there was really like? Maybe you were young. Maybe you thought there would always be time. And then one day, there wasn't.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, many Greeks left because work was scarce and they hoped to build a more secure future. Some crossed the Atlantic to the United States, planning to earn money and return. In Greek, there's a word for life far from home: ξενιτιά. It's more than a destination on a map. It's the distance between the person who leaves and the people who stay. The Greece people remembered didn't stay frozen exactly as they'd left it. It changed with their new lives.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: The people who left Greece didn't carry an entire country with them in a suitcase. They carried pieces of a life, and built something new from them. Quoted from the film's approved narration.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: Have you ever heard someone in your family mention a village in Greece, or an island, and realized you never asked what life there was really like? Maybe you were young. Maybe you thought there would always be time. And then one day, there wasn't. You remember the name of the place. Maybe you even know where it is on a map. But what was an ordinary day like there? Who lived next door? Where did everyone gather? What did home mean to them? We don't always think to ask those questions when the people who know the answers are sitting right beside us. And for so many Greek families, there's another question underneath all of them. Why did they leave? There isn't one answer. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, many Greeks left because work was scarce and they hoped to build a more secure future.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: Some crossed the Atlantic to the United States, planning to earn money and return. Later, the hardship and upheaval surrounding the Second World War and the Greek Civil War shaped another generation's decisions. Greeks also made new lives in Australia, Canada, Germany, and elsewhere. Different years. Different destinations. Different reasons. And not everyone who left had the same experience. Some traveled alone. Some followed relatives who had already gone. Some returned to Greece.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: Others expected to. They never did. Imagine making that decision without knowing how long you'd be away. What would you take? Clothes. Papers. An address written down carefully. Maybe a photograph. But the hardest things to leave weren't always things you could pack. The voices you heard every day. The familiar walk through your neighborhood. The people who knew your family before you were born. In Greek, there's a word for life far from home: ξενιτιά.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: It's more than a destination on a map. It's the distance between the person who leaves and the people who stay. In Epirus, traditional songs spoke of that separation. One is called Ξενιτεμένο μου πουλί. It means, roughly, my bird, far from home. And that part of the story matters, too. For every person beginning again somewhere else, there could be people back home waiting for news, a letter, or the next visit.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: Today, we might find a trace of that journey in an old passenger list. A name. An age. A place of origin. A destination. At first, it's just a document. Until you recognize the name. Maybe the spelling is different. Maybe there's a village nobody ever mentioned. Maybe an address points to a relative who arrived earlier. One small detail can bring you closer to someone you thought you knew only through family stories.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: But a passenger list tells you where a person was going. It doesn't tell you what happened when they got there. Think about arriving in a place where the language is unfamiliar. You need work. Somewhere to live. You have to learn how things are done. Even the little things nobody explains. And you still have people back home wondering how you're getting along. For many newcomers, other Greeks helped make that first step less lonely.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: Someone might know about a job. Someone might offer a place to stay or introduce you to a neighborhood, a church, or a familiar shop. Over time, communities took shape. In Chicago, and in cities across the world, Greeks opened businesses, formed associations, built churches, and found ways to gather. Those places weren't just reminders of home. They were part of making a new home. And something interesting happened along the way.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: The Greece people remembered didn't stay frozen exactly as they'd left it. It changed with their new lives. A family might speak Greek at home and English at work. Children might grow up with customs their classmates didn't know. Holidays and celebrations might look familiar, but take place thousands of miles from the village where their parents grew up. It wasn't always easy to balance those worlds. But you could hear that connection in a greeting.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: See it in an icon on the wall. Taste it in something made for a family gathering. And before long, those ordinary details became part of someone else's childhood.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: Maybe that's the part of this story you recognize. The next generation didn't necessarily remember the journey. They remembered the people who made a life after it. A grandparent calling them by a nickname nobody else used. Tavli dice hitting the table. A komboloi clicking in someone's hand. The smell of coffee in the kitchen. A familiar expression in Greek that everybody understood, even if nobody could explain it in English.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: Maybe there was an icon in the corner of the room. A name-day call. A meal that appeared every time the family came together. Or a song that made everyone stop talking for a moment, and then start singing. If you've watched My Big Fat Greek Wedding, you know the exaggerated version of Greek family life: the relatives, the food, everyone having an opinion. It's a comedy. But for some people, there was something recognizable underneath the jokes.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: Of course, no two families were the same. Some children learned Greek. Others understood more than they could speak. Some families were deeply involved in church and community life. Others kept only a few customs, or made entirely new ones. And that doesn't make one family's story more Greek than another's. What stayed was often what fit into everyday life. A recipe learned by watching, not measuring. A story told at the table.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: A place name mentioned so often you felt you knew it, even if you'd never been there. When we're young, these things can seem so ordinary that we barely notice them. Then years pass. We get older. We begin asking different questions. Who were our parents and grandparents before they became the people we knew? What did they give up? What did they hope for? What was their home like before ours?

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: Maybe you know the island, but not the village. Maybe there's a face in an old photograph and nobody remembers the name. Maybe you can make the dish, but you don't know who taught it to the person who taught you. And suddenly, something familiar becomes a mystery. That feeling isn't limited to Greek families. It's one of the ways we discover that our own lives are part of a much longer story.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: The good news is, we don't need every answer to begin. We can start with one question. Ask someone where the family came from. Not just Greece. Which town, which village, which neighborhood? Ask who left first. Who stayed behind. Whether anyone went back. Look through photographs together. Write down the names while someone still remembers them. And ask about the little things. The words people used. The games they played.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: The meals they made without recipes. Sometimes a memory leads to a document. Sometimes a document leads to another question. And sometimes we won't find the answer. We shouldn't invent one. The people who left Greece didn't carry an entire country with them in a suitcase. They carried pieces of a life, and built something new from them. Their children carried different pieces. And so did the generations after that. Some traditions survived. Some changed. Others faded. But Greek culture didn't end when people crossed a border. It continued in the homes they made, the communities they built, and the things they passed on, sometimes without even realizing it. We don't have to recreate the past to feel connected to it. We can listen. We can ask. We can learn where those familiar pieces came from. Maybe for you it begins with a photograph.

passages.t: The Greeks Who Left, and the Greece They Carried
passages.x: Questions to start a conversation at your own table. What did our family bring with them when they left Greece? What did our grandparents miss most about home? Which traditions did our family keep after arriving in a new country?

passages.t: The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was
passages.x: In 1964, Zorba the Greek gave audiences around the world an image of Greece that would become almost impossible to separate from the country itself. Greece already had more dances than Hollywood could ever fit into one film. Greek dance isn't decoration sitting on top of a Greek culture. It's one of the places culture was stored. And nobody packs a dance into a suitcase. People carried it another way. They remember it. They teach it. A child watches a parent. A grandchild watches a grandparent.

passages.x: Something invented can become tradition. Something old can change. And something genuinely ancient can disappear completely if nobody teaches it. Age doesn't guarantee survival. People do. Quoted from the film's recorded narration.

passages.t: The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was
passages.x: Which sounds almost ridiculous, because Greece already had more dances than Hollywood could ever fit into one film. We talk about Greek dancing, as if somebody designed one set of steps for the entire country, they didn't. Greece has regions, islands, mountains, villages, refugee communities, local histories, and those histories move differently. On the mainland, traditions like Tsamiko developed their own regional identities. Crete has dances like Pentozali. Across the Dodecanese and other islands, you find different forms of sousta.

passages.t: The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was
passages.x: Pontic Greek communities preserve completely different movement traditions. And even dances carrying the same name can change from one community to another. That's important. Because the map matters. A dance wasn't just something people performed. It could tell you where people came from, who they celebrated with, what community they belonged to. Sometimes even which village taught them the steps. Greek dance isn't decoration sitting on top of a Greek culture. It's one of the places culture was stored.

passages.t: The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was
passages.h: Nobody packs a dance into a suitcase
passages.x: But maps have a problem. People leave them. War. Poverty. Displacement. Work. Opportunity. Sometimes survival. For generations, Greeks left villages, islands, and cities and built lives somewhere else. Sometimes somewhere else in Greece. Sometimes much further. Europe, Australia, Canada, the United States. And nobody packs a dance into a suitcase. There isn't a box marked “dance.” Family, photographs, clothes, important documents, 300 years of village dancing. People carried it another way. They remember it. They teach it.

passages.t: The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was
passages.h: Nobody packs a dance into a suitcase
passages.x: One person watches another. A child watches a parent. A grandchild watches a grandparent. Someone gets pulled onto a dance floor at a wedding. Someone stands at the edge of a church festival until an uncle grabs their arm and says, come on. And suddenly something that once belonged to a particular place can survive thousands of miles away from it. Because now it isn't simply dancing. It's evidence of where you came from.

passages.t: The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was
passages.x: But then there's a dance that doesn't work anything like the image Hollywood would give it and show to the world. One dancer. No line of people moving together. No fixed sequence that everybody has to copy. No smiling roll of tourists with their arms across each other's shoulders. Zeibekiko, usually described as a solo improvisational dance. Zeibekiko leaves far more to the individual dancer. But history is much harder to fit into a neat sentence.

passages.t: The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was
passages.x: Rebetiko developed in the urban world of the early 20th century Greece. Ports, working class neighborhoods, refugee communities, people living at the edges of respectable society. And the songs weren't exactly tourism advertisements. Love, hardship, prison, drugs, poverty, longing, everyday life. Rebetiko absorbed influence from different communities and musical traditions and became part of the changing sound of urban Greece. Zeibekiko became deeply associated with that world.

passages.t: The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was
passages.h: Zorba, and a ban at home
passages.x: Outside the country: Zorba, the beach, the music, the dance, freedom. Inside Greece, something much more complicated. And while governments could censor music, they couldn't completely control what happened next. Because Greek culture had already traveled far beyond Greece.

passages.t: The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was
passages.x: Come to Chicago, thousands of miles from Epirus, from Crete, from the islands, from Pontus. A child walks into a Greek church hall or cultural center. Maybe that child was born in Illinois. Maybe their parents were too. Maybe their Greek isn't perfect. Maybe they've never lived in the village their family came from. Maybe they've never even seen it. But somebody starts the music and somebody teaches them the steps. Organizations like the Orpheus Hellenic Folklore Society here in the Chicago area teach Greek dances and music to adults and younger generations preserving repertoire from regions across Greece.

passages.t: The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was
passages.x: Think about what that actually means. Something once tied closely to geography survives after the geography is gone. For a few minutes, Epirus can exist in Illinois. Crete can exist here. The islands can exist here. Pontus can exist here. Not because Illinois suddenly became Greece. Because somebody remembered and somebody taught the next person.

passages.t: The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was
passages.x: Growing up, I thought Greek dancing was just something Greeks did. Weddings, festivals, church events. Music starts. Everybody gets up. Never thought very hard about why. I definitely never thought of it as an archive. But that's what I started to see. An archive that doesn't sit on a shelf, it lives in people. Every time someone remembers the steps, something survives. Every time somebody teaches a child, something moves forward. Every time nobody teaches the next person, something gets a little closer to disappearing.

passages.t: The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was
passages.x: Something invented can become tradition. Something old can change. Something imported can be adapted. Something forgotten can be revived. And something genuinely ancient can disappear completely if nobody teaches it. Age doesn't guarantee survival. People do. So maybe the question isn't “what's the real Greek dance?” There are too many answers. The better question is: who taught you yours? Because somewhere behind those steps is a place. A family, a migration, a piece of history.

passages.t: The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was
passages.x: And somebody who decided it was worth remembering. Maybe it was your father, your mother, your grandparents, an uncle, a teacher. Someone at a church festival who grabbed your hand and pulled you into the line. And maybe you never asked them where they learned it. Ask them while you still can. Because one day somebody younger may ask you the same question. And then it'll be your turn to remember. That's the part I was never taught.

passages.t: The Greek Dance That Wasn't Real… Until It Was
passages.x: And I'm starting to think that this part's worth preserving. This is Krios, the living story of Greek civilization. Preserve, teach, understand, connect. Pass this forward. The narration as spoken in the film, from its published English captions.

passages.t: Ohi Day, October 28: what happened in 1940 and how Greeks remember it
passages.x: On October 28, Greeks remember the morning in 1940 when Greece refused Italy's ultimatum and went to war. It is a national holiday in Greece and in Cyprus.

passages.t: Ohi Day, October 28: what happened in 1940 and how Greeks remember it
passages.x: Greeks marked the anniversary even under occupation, and after liberation it became a national holiday. In Thessaloniki, soldiers march before the President of the Republic. In towns and villages across Greece, schoolchildren parade under blue-and-white flags. On the same day the Church of Greece celebrates the Protection of the Theotokos (Αγία Σκέπη), a feast it placed on October 28 in 1952. It is a church feast, separate from the national commemoration.

passages.t: What does ξενιτιά (xenitia) mean?
passages.x: ξενιτιά is the Greek word for life far from home. It is more than a place on a map. It is the distance between the person who leaves and the people who stay behind, waiting for news, a letter or the next visit. Traditional songs from Epirus spoke of that separation. One is called Ξενιτεμένο μου πουλί, which means, roughly, my bird, far from home. Drawn from the KRIOS film and its research notes.

passages.t: What is a Greek spoon sweet?
passages.h: What is a Greek spoon sweet?
passages.x: A spoon sweet, glyko tou koutaliou in Greek, is fruit preserved in thick syrup. It is served on a small spoon, traditionally to every guest who arrives at a Greek home, as a gesture of hospitality. Almost any fruit can be used: sour cherries, quince, figs, citrus peel, even young walnuts. For many families it is a taste of childhood, kept in a jar in the cupboard for visitors.

passages.t: Who was Athanasios Diakos?
passages.x: Athanasios Diakos was a Greek commander of the War of Independence. He had trained as a deacon, which is where the name Diakos comes from, before becoming a klepht, one of the mountain fighters who resisted Ottoman rule. In April 1821 he held the bridge of Alamana, near Thermopylae, against a much larger Ottoman force. Captured after the battle, he was offered his life if he converted to Islam. He refused and was executed. A monument to him stands at Thermopylae, near the monument to Leonidas.

passages.t: Who was Laskarina Bouboulina?
passages.x: Laskarina Bouboulina was a shipowner from Spetses and a naval commander in the Greek War of Independence of 1821. After the deaths of her two husbands she managed their fortune and fleet herself. She had the warship Agamemnon built and commanded it in the blockade of Nafplio. She was even arrested for a time by the revolutionary leadership, her own side, before being released.

passages.t: Who were the Vallahades?
passages.x: The Vallahades were Greek-speaking Muslims of western Macedonia, around Anaselitsa and Grevena. Their ancestors converted to Islam under Ottoman rule, but the community kept the Greek language and much of its Greek culture for generations. In the population exchange between Greece and Turkey in 1923, people were sorted by religion, not language. The Vallahades were classified as Muslims and sent to Turkey.

passages.t: Why are there so many Greeks in Tarpon Springs, Florida?
passages.h: Why are there so many Greeks in Tarpon Springs, Florida?
passages.x: In 1905 John Cocoris recruited Greek sponge divers to work the sponge beds off the Florida coast, bringing diving suits and methods the local industry had never used. Divers came first from Aegina and Hydra, then from the Dodecanese islands of Kalymnos, Symi and Halki. The community built a church, a sponge exchange and a Greek town around the docks. Today Tarpon Springs has the highest percentage of Greek-Americans of any city in the United States, and its Epiphany cross dive is famous across the country.

passages.t: Why did so many Greeks emigrate?
passages.h: Why did so many Greeks emigrate?
passages.x: There isn't one answer. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, many Greeks left because work was scarce. The first wave followed the economic crisis of 1893, when currant export prices collapsed. Most went to the United States and Egypt, and many planned to earn money and return. A second wave, mainly between 1950 and 1974, followed the hardship of the Second World War and the Greek Civil War. More than a million Greeks left, most to Western Europe, the United States, Canada and Australia. Almost half of them had returned to Greece by 1985.
